claim: Lung cancer is the second most common type of cancer.
source: Lung cancer is the second most common type of cancer.
evidence: This is a statement of fact presented in the introduction without supporting data in the manuscript itself.

claim: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men and women.
source: it is still by far the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men and women, resulting in more deaths than colon, breast, and prostate cancer combined (American Cancer Society, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Cancer Society, 2019.

claim: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 84% of lung cancer cases.
source: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, accounting for 84% of lung cancer cases.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adenocarcinoma accounts for 50% of all NSCLCs.
source: Within this cancer type, adenocarcinoma is the most frequent subtype, accounting for 50% of all NSCLCs (Davidson et al., 2013; Langer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2013 and Langer et al., 2010.

claim: Most cases of lung cancer are diagnosed at late-stage when there is regional or distant spread of the disease.
source: Most cases of lung cancer are diagnosed at late-stage—when there is regional or distant spread of the disease—at which time treatment options are limited (Heist and Engelman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heist and Engelman, 2012.

claim: The 5-year survival rates for late-stage (regional or distant) NSCLC are 37–9%, respectively.
source: Despite advances in lung cancer therapy, the 5-year survival rates for late-stage (i.e. regional or distant) NSCLC are 37–9%, respectively (American Cancer Society, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Cancer Society, 2024.

claim: Msi2 has been shown to be critical in development as well as advanced cancers.
source: The stem cell fate determinant Musashi-2 (Msi2) is one such signal that has been shown to be critical in development as well as advanced cancers (Fox et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010; Koechlein et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fox et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010; Koechlein et al., 2016.

claim: Msi2 has been reported to be overexpressed in human lung adenocarcinoma and regional metastases.
source: Msi2 has been reported to be overexpressed in human lung adenocarcinoma and regional metastases, and its inhibition in human cell lines has been shown to reduce invasive and metastatic potential in vitro (Kudinov et al., 2016; Moreira et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kudinov et al., 2016 and Moreira et al., 2010.

claim: Msi2 is expressed in 39% of Lin−EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells.
source: We used a Msi2eGFP/+ knock-in reporter mouse to track endogenous Msi2 expression (Fox et al., 2016), and found that Msi2 is expressed in 39% of Lin−EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using Msi2 reporter mice.

claim: Msi2 is expressed in 37% of cells enriched for Club/BASC cells.
source: and, more specifically, in 37% of cells enriched for Club/BASC cells and 26% of cells enriched for AT2 cells—the known stem cell populations of the distal lung (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Msi2 is expressed in 26% of cells enriched for AT2 cells.
source: and, more specifically, in 37% of cells enriched for Club/BASC cells and 26% of cells enriched for AT2 cells—the known stem cell populations of the distal lung (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Widespread expression of Msi2 was often observed in lung adenocarcinomas formed in KrasG12D/+; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mice.
source: Interestingly, although Msi2 expression could only be detected in a fraction of distal lung stem cells, widespread expression of Msi2 was often observed in lung adenocarcinomas formed in KrasG12D/+; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Msi2+ cells had a sixfold increase in sphere-forming capacity at primary passage compared to Msi2− cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, Msi2+ cells had enhanced sphere-forming capacity, with a sixfold increase in sphere-forming observed at primary passage, and this capacity was retained for up to four passages (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spheres isolated from Msi2+ cells and transplanted subcutaneously into immunocompromised mice developed Msi2-expressing tumors in vivo.
source: Furthermore, spheres that were isolated and transplanted subcutaneously into the flanks of immunocompromised mice developed Msi2-expressing tumors in vivo as well as metastatic lesions in the lung, demonstrating that the observed sphere-forming capacity is reflective of tumorigenicity and not merely stem cell capacity (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Spheres from Msi2+ cells transplanted subcutaneously developed metastatic lesions in the lung.
source: Furthermore, spheres that were isolated and transplanted subcutaneously into the flanks of immunocompromised mice developed Msi2-expressing tumors in vivo as well as metastatic lesions in the lung, demonstrating that the observed sphere-forming capacity is reflective of tumorigenicity and not merely stem cell capacity (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Msi2+ cells are transcriptionally distinct from Msi2− cells.
source: Interestingly, the differentially expressed gene profile showed that Msi2+ cells are transcriptionally distinct from Msi2− cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Msi2+ cells are significantly enriched for signatures related to developmental and stem cell signaling.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) further revealed that Msi2+ cells are significantly enriched for signatures related to developmental and stem cell signaling, consistent with the known role of Msi2 as a critical regulator of the stem cell state (Okano et al., 2002; Hope et al., 2010; Kharas et al., 2010), as well as signatures related to oncogenic signaling and therapy resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D) which are associated with aggressive cancers.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D and citations to Okano et al., 2002; Hope et al., 2010; Kharas et al., 2010.

claim: Msi2+ cells are significantly enriched for signatures related to oncogenic signaling and therapy resistance.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) further revealed that Msi2+ cells are significantly enriched for signatures related to developmental and stem cell signaling, consistent with the known role of Msi2 as a critical regulator of the stem cell state (Okano et al., 2002; Hope et al., 2010; Kharas et al., 2010), as well as signatures related to oncogenic signaling and therapy resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D) which are associated with aggressive cancers.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Over 1900 differentially expressed genes were found to be enriched in the Msi2+ population.
source: Over 1900 differentially expressed genes were found to be enriched in the Msi2+ population.
evidence: Stated as a result from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: Loss of Msi2 led to the formation of significantly fewer (84%) tumor lesions in Msi2−/− KP mice compared to wild-type KP mice at a 14-week midpoint.
source: Importantly, loss of Msi2 led to the formation of significantly fewer (84%) tumor lesions as well as a significantly lower (85%) overall tumor burden in the lung at a 14-week midpoint (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Loss of Msi2 led to a significantly lower (85%) overall tumor burden in Msi2−/− KP mice compared to wild-type KP mice at a 14-week midpoint.
source: Importantly, loss of Msi2 led to the formation of significantly fewer (84%) tumor lesions as well as a significantly lower (85%) overall tumor burden in the lung at a 14-week midpoint (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Loss of Msi2 resulted in a significant decrease in the frequency of mid- and high-grade tumors (45–54%).
source: Furthermore, while there was no difference in the frequency of low-grade tumors, there was a significant decrease in the frequency of mid- and high-grade tumors (45–54%), suggesting that loss of Msi2 delayed tumor progression from low to high grade (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Msi2−/− KP mice infected with Ad-Cre developed tumors less frequently than wild-type KP mice (61% Msi2−/− vs 83% Msi2+/+).
source: Importantly, Msi2−/− KP mice infected with Ad-Cre developed tumors less frequently than their wild-type counterparts (61% Msi2−/− vs 83% Msi2+/+; Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Msi2−/− KP mice displayed a significant increase in overall survival compared to Msi2+/+ KP mice, with median survival of 428 days vs 209 days.
source: Additionally, Msi2−/− KP mice displayed a significant increase in overall survival compared to Msi2+/+ KP mice. Msi2+/+ KP mice had a median survival of 209 days while the Msi2−/− KP mice had a median survival of 428 days, reflecting a twofold increase in survival (p = 0.04, Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental survival data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The majority of lung tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were found to express Msi2.
source: Notably, the majority of lung tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were found to express Msi2, suggesting that the tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were escapers that re-expressed Msi2, underscoring the dependency on Msi2 signaling for tumor formation (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Loss of Msi2 led to a significant decrease (75%) in tumorsphere formation in vitro in KP cell lines.
source: Importantly, loss of Msi2 led to a significant decrease (75%) in tumorsphere formation in vitro, suggesting that Msi2 is required for tumor cell propagation (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Msi2-knockdown KP tumors had significantly reduced (89%) tumor cell numbers in vivo.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the Msi2-knockdown tumors had significantly reduced (89%) tumor cell numbers (Figure 4C, D), indicating that established tumors remain dependent on Msi2 signaling for growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Inhibition of Msi2 in patient-derived xenografts led to tumors that were 64–88% smaller than control tumors at endpoint.
source: Importantly, although an equivalent number of shControl and shMsi2 cells were transplanted into recipient mice, there was a notable delay in the growth of Msi2-knockdown tumors, which were 64–88% smaller than control tumors at endpoint (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibition of Msi2 in lung cancer cells had a significant impact on developmental and stem cell signaling programs and genes.
source: Consistent with the role of Msi2 in stem cell maintenance, the inhibition of Msi2 in lung cancer cells had a significant impact on developmental and stem cell signaling programs and genes, this included Porcn, the transcription regulator Nupr1, and the NuRD complex member Mbd3, which have been shown to play a role in the maintenance of the stem cell state (Figure 5B, C; Clevers et al., 2014; Tammela et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Loughran et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B, C and citations to Clevers et al., 2014; Tammela et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Loughran et al., 2017.

claim: Msi2 impacted DNA repair genes including Brca1, Atm, and several Fanconi anemia complementation group genes.
source: In addition, Msi2 impacted a broad range of other signaling programs and their associated genes, including DNA repair and metabolism. DNA repair genes included Brca1, Atm, and several Fanconi anemia complementation group genes (Scully et al., 1997; Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003; Walden and Deans, 2014)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis and citations to Scully et al., 1997; Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003; Walden and Deans, 2014.

claim: Msi2 impacted metabolism programs including the gluconeogenesis enzyme Pck2, several isoforms of Cpt1, and the glutamate dehydrogenase Glud1.
source: and metabolism programs included the gluconeogenesis enzyme Pck2, which has been shown to promote lung cancer cell survival in low glucose conditions, several isoforms of Cpt1, a key regulator in fatty acid oxidation known to promote tumor growth in a variety of cancers, and the glutamate dehydrogenase Glud1, which has been shown to promote tumorigenesis in lung cancer xenografts (Figure 5D–G; Leithner et al., 2015; Kuo and Ann, 2018; Jin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5D-G and citations to Leithner et al., 2015; Kuo and Ann, 2018; Jin et al., 2015.

claim: Known regulators of lung adenocarcinoma such as Gli1, βIII tubulin (Tubb3), and CC Chemokine Receptor 1 (Ccr1) were found to be significantly downregulated following Msi2 inhibition.
source: Interestingly, several known regulators of lung adenocarcinoma such as Gli1, a canonical downstream effector of the Hedgehog signaling pathway, βIII tubulin (Tubb3), and CC Chemokine Receptor 1 (Ccr1) were found to be significantly downregulated following Msi2 inhibition as well (Figure 5H; Rentas et al., 2016; Song et al., 2011; Han et al., 2017; Po et al., 2017; Avis et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2009a; Wang et al., 2009b; Stallings-Mann et al., 2012; McCarroll et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5H and multiple citations.

claim: Inhibition of Ptgds, Arl2bp, Rnf157, and Syt11 led to a significant decrease (88–98%) in the formation of tumor spheres in vitro.
source: To test whether these genes regulate tumor cell growth we knocked down each of these genes (Ptgds, Arl2bp, Rnf157, and Syt11) in the KP cell line. Inhibition of each target led to a significant decrease (88–98%) in the formation of tumor spheres in vitro (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Msi2 signaling has been shown to contribute to colon adenomas.
source: The stem cell fate determinant Msi2 is commonly found to be expressed in carcinomas (Moreira et al., 2010; Kharas and Lengner, 2017; Uhlén et al., 2015; Uhlen et al., 2010) and Msi signaling has been shown to contribute to colon adenomas (Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Msi2 maintains the aggressive, undifferentiated state in hematologic malignancies and pancreatic cancer.
source: and Msi signaling has been shown to contribute to colon adenomas (Wang et al., 2015) and maintain the aggressive, undifferentiated state in hematologic malignancies and pancreatic cancer (Ito et al., 2010; Fox et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito et al., 2010 and Fox et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of Msi2 at initiation significantly impaired tumor incidence in the KP mouse model.
source: Using the well-established KrasG12D; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (Jackson et al., 2005), we created a Msi2-knockout lung adenocarcinoma model and found that deletion of Msi2 at initiation significantly impaired tumor incidence, reduced tumor burden and progression, and cumulatively led to a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the KP mouse model and citation to Jackson et al., 2005.

claim: Deletion of Msi2 at initiation reduced tumor burden in the KP mouse model.
source: Using the well-established KrasG12D; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (Jackson et al., 2005), we created a Msi2-knockout lung adenocarcinoma model and found that deletion of Msi2 at initiation significantly impaired tumor incidence, reduced tumor burden and progression, and cumulatively led to a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the KP mouse model and citation to Jackson et al., 2005.

claim: Deletion of Msi2 at initiation reduced tumor progression in the KP mouse model.
source: Using the well-established KrasG12D; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (Jackson et al., 2005), we created a Msi2-knockout lung adenocarcinoma model and found that deletion of Msi2 at initiation significantly impaired tumor incidence, reduced tumor burden and progression, and cumulatively led to a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the KP mouse model and citation to Jackson et al., 2005.

claim: Deletion of Msi2 at initiation led to a doubling of median survival in the KP mouse model.
source: Using the well-established KrasG12D; Trp53fl/fl (KP) mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (Jackson et al., 2005), we created a Msi2-knockout lung adenocarcinoma model and found that deletion of Msi2 at initiation significantly impaired tumor incidence, reduced tumor burden and progression, and cumulatively led to a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the KP mouse model and citation to Jackson et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of Msi2 impaired propagation of established KP tumors in vitro.
source: Furthermore, loss of Msi2 impaired propagation of established KP tumors in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tumorsphere assays.

claim: Loss of Msi2 impaired propagation of established KP tumors in vivo.
source: Furthermore, loss of Msi2 impaired propagation of established KP tumors in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flank transplant assays.

claim: Patient-derived xenografts have proven to be a highly valuable tool for understanding the biology of human cancers.
source: In order to determine whether these findings were relevant for the human disease, we used PDXs, which have proven to be a highly valuable tool for understanding the biology of human cancers and have been shown to faithfully predict therapeutic response in a majority of patients (Tentler et al., 2012; Siolas and Hannon, 2013; Hidalgo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tentler et al., 2012; Siolas and Hannon, 2013; Hidalgo et al., 2014.

claim: Patient-derived xenografts have been shown to faithfully predict therapeutic response in a majority of patients.
source: In order to determine whether these findings were relevant for the human disease, we used PDXs, which have proven to be a highly valuable tool for understanding the biology of human cancers and have been shown to faithfully predict therapeutic response in a majority of patients (Tentler et al., 2012; Siolas and Hannon, 2013; Hidalgo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tentler et al., 2012; Siolas and Hannon, 2013; Hidalgo et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of Msi2 in PDXs led to impaired tumor growth in vivo.
source: Inhibition of Msi2 in PDXs also led to impaired tumor growth in vivo, suggesting that dependence on Msi2 is conserved in human lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from PDX experiments.

claim: Msi2 is expressed in a subpopulation of distal lung stem cells.
source: In this context, our work sheds new light on such signals required at initiation as we found that Msi2 is expressed in a subpopulation of distal lung stem cells, that cells expressing Msi2 are preferentially sensitive to transformation, and that its genetic ablation leads to a marked decrease in tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Msi2 reporter mice.

claim: Cells expressing Msi2 are preferentially sensitive to transformation.
source: In this context, our work sheds new light on such signals required at initiation as we found that Msi2 is expressed in a subpopulation of distal lung stem cells, that cells expressing Msi2 are preferentially sensitive to transformation, and that its genetic ablation leads to a marked decrease in tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tumorsphere and transplant assays.

claim: Genetic ablation of Msi2 leads to a marked decrease in tumor initiation.
source: In this context, our work sheds new light on such signals required at initiation as we found that Msi2 is expressed in a subpopulation of distal lung stem cells, that cells expressing Msi2 are preferentially sensitive to transformation, and that its genetic ablation leads to a marked decrease in tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Msi2 knockout KP mice.

claim: Genetic ablation of Msi2 leads to a marked decrease in tumor progression.
source: In this context, our work sheds new light on such signals required at initiation as we found that Msi2 is expressed in a subpopulation of distal lung stem cells, that cells expressing Msi2 are preferentially sensitive to transformation, and that its genetic ablation leads to a marked decrease in tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Msi2 knockout KP mice.

claim: Msi2 may act in part as a regulator of the stem cell state.
source: Here, our RNAseq analysis suggests that Msi2 may act in part as a regulator of the stem cell state.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis showing impact on stem cell signaling programs.

claim: The role of Msi2 may extend to the regulation of processes crucial for tumor growth, such as metabolism and DNA repair.
source: Interestingly, this analysis also showed that the role of Msi2 may extend to the regulation of processes crucial for tumor growth, such as metabolism and DNA repair, thus placing it upstream of multiple potent oncogenic signals.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis showing impact on metabolism and DNA repair pathways.

claim: Ptgds has been shown previously to be expressed in human lung tumors.
source: Previous work has shown that Ptgds indirectly facilitates phosphorylated Sox9 nuclear translocation via activation of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) (Malki et al., 2005) and is important in the development of Sertoli cells. While Ptgds has been shown previously to be expressed in human lung tumors (Ragolia et al., 2010) our work is the first to identify a functional role of Ptgds in lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ragolia et al., 2010.

claim: Arl2bp directly binds to the STAT3 transcription factor, which maintains STAT3's phosphorylation status and its localization in the nucleus.
source: As a regulator of STAT3 signaling, Arl2bp directly binds to the STAT3 transcription factor, which maintains STAT3's phosphorylation status and its localization in the nucleus (Muromoto et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muromoto et al., 2008.

claim: STAT3 activity has been implicated in NSCLC.
source: STAT3 activity has been implicated in NSCLC (Mohrherr et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mohrherr et al., 2020.

claim: Rnf157 has been implicated in neuronal cell survival and dendrite growth.
source: Lastly, both Rnf157 and Syt11 are predominantly expressed in the brain and have been implicated in neuronal cell survival and dendrite growth and neuronal vesicular trafficking, respectively (Matz et al., 2015; Shimojo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matz et al., 2015.

claim: Syt11 has been implicated in neuronal vesicular trafficking.
source: Lastly, both Rnf157 and Syt11 are predominantly expressed in the brain and have been implicated in neuronal cell survival and dendrite growth and neuronal vesicular trafficking, respectively (Matz et al., 2015; Shimojo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shimojo et al., 2019.

claim: The treatment of lung cancer has evolved to incorporate the use of targeted therapies and immunotherapy in combination with the standard cytotoxic regimen.
source: While early treatment approaches centered principally on the use of cytotoxic agents, the treatment of lung cancer has evolved to incorporate the use of targeted therapies and immunotherapy, when appropriate, in combination with the standard cytotoxic regimen (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herbst et al., 2018.

claim: Msi2 plays a dual role in lung adenocarcinoma, acting as a signal that is essential for initiation and continues to be required post-establishment.
source: Using Msi2 knock-in reporter mice and Msi2 conditional knockout mice, we show that Msi2 plays a dual role in lung adenocarcinoma, acting as a signal that not only is essential for initiation, but one that continues to be required post-establishment in both genetically engineered mouse models and in PDXs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple mouse models and PDXs.

claim: Msi2 can trigger a range of pathways critical for tumor growth, including several new effectors of lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Finally, using RNA-sequencing (RNAseq) analysis we show that Msi2 can trigger a range of pathways critical for tumor growth, including several new effectors of lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis and functional validation experiments.

claim: Msi2 is a critical regulator of lung adenocarcinoma.
source: These findings suggest that Msi2 is a critical regulator of lung adenocarcinoma and offer new insight into the signals that facilitate transformation and support disease progression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic deletion of Msi2 in an autochthonous Ras/p53-driven lung cancer model resulted in a marked reduction of tumor burden.
source: Consistent with this, genetic deletion of Msi2 in an autochthonous Ras/p53-driven lung cancer model resulted in a marked reduction of tumor burden, delayed progression, and a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Msi2 knockout KP mice.

claim: Genetic deletion of Msi2 in an autochthonous Ras/p53-driven lung cancer model resulted in delayed progression.
source: Consistent with this, genetic deletion of Msi2 in an autochthonous Ras/p53-driven lung cancer model resulted in a marked reduction of tumor burden, delayed progression, and a doubling of median survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Msi2 knockout KP mice.

claim: Msi2 triggered a broad range of pathways critical for tumor growth.
source: Mechanistically, Msi2 triggered a broad range of pathways critical for tumor growth, including several novel effectors of lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis showing impact on multiple signaling pathways.

claim: Msi2-expressing cells in normal lung epithelia are enriched for genes involved in developmental and stem cell signaling.
source: In line with the GSEA results, these enriched genes included those involved in developmental and stem cell signaling (such as Dll1, Jag2, and Notch3) (Kumar et al., 2019; Than-Trong et al., 2018; Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and citations to Kumar et al., 2019; Than-Trong et al., 2018; Ntziachristos et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011.

claim: Msi2-expressing cells in normal lung epithelia are enriched for genes involved in oncogenic signaling.
source: oncogenic signaling (such as Akt3, Ret, Myb, and Fos) (Chin et al., 2014; Mulligan, 2014; Ramsay and Gonda, 2008; Muhammad et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and citations to Chin et al., 2014; Mulligan, 2014; Ramsay and Gonda, 2008; Muhammad et al., 2017.

claim: Msi2-expressing cells in normal lung epithelia are enriched for genes involved in therapy resistance.
source: and therapy resistance (such as Axl, Egr1, and several glutathione S transferases implicated in platinum drug resistance including Gstp1 and Gsta2) (Pinato et al., 2019; Allocati et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017; Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2F-H and citations to Pinato et al., 2019; Allocati et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: The transcriptional landscape of Msi2-expressing cells is enriched in signaling programs that are conducive to tumorigenesis.
source: These findings suggest that prior to tumor initiation, the transcriptional landscape of Msi2-expressing cells is enriched in signaling programs that are conducive to tumorigenesis, which may make them uniquely poised for transformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq analysis of Msi2+ cells.

claim: Loss of Msi2 delayed tumor progression from low to high grade.
source: Furthermore, while there was no difference in the frequency of low-grade tumors, there was a significant decrease in the frequency of mid- and high-grade tumors (45–54%), suggesting that loss of Msi2 delayed tumor progression from low to high grade (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were escapers that re-expressed Msi2.
source: Notably, the majority of lung tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were found to express Msi2, suggesting that the tumors that formed in Msi2−/− KP mice were escapers that re-expressed Msi2, underscoring the dependency on Msi2 signaling for tumor formation (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Msi2−/− tumors express Msi2.

claim: Established tumors remain dependent on Msi2 signaling for growth.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the Msi2-knockdown tumors had significantly reduced (89%) tumor cell numbers (Figure 4C, D), indicating that established tumors remain dependent on Msi2 signaling for growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Dependence on Msi2 is conserved in human lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Inhibition of Msi2 in PDXs also led to impaired tumor growth in vivo, suggesting that dependence on Msi2 is conserved in human lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PDX experimental data.

claim: Msi2 is placed upstream of multiple potent oncogenic signals.
source: Interestingly, this analysis also showed that the role of Msi2 may extend to the regulation of processes crucial for tumor growth, such as metabolism and DNA repair, thus placing it upstream of multiple potent oncogenic signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq analysis showing Msi2's impact on multiple pathways.

claim: Ptgds, Arl2bp, Rnf157, and Syt11 are downstream effectors of Msi2 activity.
source: These findings not only identify these genes as downstream effectors of Msi2 activity but more generally show that this dataset could be an important resource to identify new regulators of lung adenocarcinoma growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq data showing these genes are downregulated by Msi2 loss and functional validation.

claim: The RNAseq dataset could be an important resource to identify new regulators of lung adenocarcinoma growth.
source: These findings not only identify these genes as downstream effectors of Msi2 activity but more generally show that this dataset could be an important resource to identify new regulators of lung adenocarcinoma growth.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential utility of the dataset.

claim: Msi2 signaling emerges as a key dependency at initiation and continues to be needed during tumor progression.
source: Here, we have used genetically engineered and autochthonous models to show that Msi2 is critically required in the development and progression of primary lung adenocarcinoma. Msi2 signaling emerges as a key dependency at initiation and continues to be needed during tumor progression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Modulating STAT3 activity through Arl2bp inhibition may provide an alternative therapeutic strategy.
source: STAT3 activity has been implicated in NSCLC (Mohrherr et al., 2020), thus modulating STAT3 activity through Arl2bp inhibition may provide an alternative therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: The findings identify a novel role for Msi2 in the growth and progression of lung adenocarcinoma.
source: The findings presented here identify a novel role for Msi2 in the growth and progression of lung adenocarcinoma and suggest that this role extends to human disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: The role of Msi2 extends to human disease.
source: The findings presented here identify a novel role for Msi2 in the growth and progression of lung adenocarcinoma and suggest that this role extends to human disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PDX experimental data.

claim: The findings identify novel effectors of lung adenocarcinoma regulated by Msi2.
source: Furthermore, these findings identify novel effectors of lung adenocarcinoma regulated by Msi2 thereby lending new insight into the mechanism by which Msi2 exerts its influence on this disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNAseq analysis and functional validation.

claim: The findings may serve to open new avenues of focus for future therapeutic strategies.
source: These new insights enhance our understanding of the biology of lung adenocarcinoma and may serve to open new avenues of focus for future therapeutic strategies.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications of the findings.

claim: Msi2 acts initially to sensitize cells to transformation.
source: Here, we have used extensive genetic modeling and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) to identify a dual role for Msi2: as a signal that acts initially to sensitize cells to transformation, and subsequently to drive tumor propagation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings from reporter mice and knockout models.

claim: Msi2 subsequently drives tumor propagation.
